kind: Hear the New Testament, and walk to the Nativity with the Church
title: Hear the New Testament, and walk to the Nativity with the Church
blurb: Purify 1.8 reads the whole New Testament aloud, verse by verse, and the day's readings with it. Toward the Nativity walks you through the forty days of the fast with the Fathers, alone or with your parish, household or friends. Every book in the reading room says where its words come from, Who said it? finds where a quote really stands, and the councils and Orthodox History come with maps.

items.text: The whole New Testament read aloud: all 260 chapters, verse by verse, with the verse being read lit as you go. Tap Listen beside a chapter's name.
Today's readings, read aloud: one tap on Today plays the day's Epistle and Gospel, only the verses the Church reads that day.
Listen with your phone locked: in the apps the reading goes on with the screen off, with play, pause and skip on the lock screen.

Reading paths: short runs through the Fathers, a day at a time. Start with The Fathers, Prayer, In sorrow, or Toward the Nativity, forty days for the Nativity Fast, offered on Today from a week before it begins.
Read together: walk a reading path with your parish, your household or friends. See who has read each day, and talk each day over.
Who said it? Paste a line that goes round under a saint's name and see where it stands, word for word, or that no Father Purify carries says it. Share the answer as a picture.
Every book in the reading room says where its words come from, and the ones checked word for word against their printed editions say so.
The Fathers on everyday struggles: anxiety, anger, grief, temptation, loneliness, despondency, pride and forgiving others, in their own words.
The councils and Orthodox History on maps, with a slider through the years, from Lyons to Moscow. On a phone the maps pan sideways, so every name can be read.

On Today: the saint of the day in their own words; on your name day, your patron's icon and words; and your departed remembered on their third, ninth and fortieth days and on the Saturdays of the Souls.
The apps open on the horizon: the cross on the night comes alive while the app loads, and the horizon rises under it before Today.
Yellow is back for highlights, and a double tap highlights a verse in the color you used last.

New writings in the reading room: St Celestine's letter to the Council of Ephesus, St Irene's letters for the Seventh Council, the sayings of St Arsenius, St Justinian's anathemas, St Tarasius's words at the Seventh Council, St Cyprian's letters on baptism, St Alexander's letter against Arius, St Ephraim's Hymns on the Nativity, St Leo's sermons on the Nativity and St Gregory's oration on the Nativity.
St Gregory the Theologian's orations: twenty-three more, the five Theological Orations among them, each read against its printed page.

St Cyril of Alexandria's Commentary on Luke, checked word for word against its sources from the first sermon to the last, with hundreds of misread words put right. His sermons on Luke 1 and 2 are on the Toward the Nativity path.
Tap a saint's name in a text to open their card, in the Lives, the councils' accounts and the heresies too.
Orthodox History: sixteen more events written in full, with pictures.

Theology by subject, with icons; twenty-one heresies, each with the words of the council that condemned it; and every council in Purify now has its texts to read, from the Seven to the Synod of Jerusalem.
The shop, redone in black and white: calmer, and easier to find things in.
Buy more, save more, in steps.
An icon's page shows its saint in their own words, and the way to their writings.
New ambience: cathedral bells, the sea, and wind.
Listen offline: in the apps, save a book's readings on your phone.
Back goes back the way you came, from a book, a plan, Settings and Account.
The Android icon is sharp at every size.
The reading room's texts were measured against the books they come from: editors' footnotes are out of the Fathers' words, and lost quotation marks are back.
Long names no longer run out of their tiles, and Discover's pictures show a soft preview while they load.
Long books like the Confessions open a book at a time, so they move smoothly on a phone, and their contents number the books as the books do.
Hymns in the library now come from public-domain service books, or say they are our English, and St Gregory Palamas's pages quote only what their sources say.
